say: Everything else in this part of the book expects you to already know why it exists. Pipeline Cinema does not. It plays a machine learning pipeline as an animation, with a narrator, for the person seeing one for the first time.
It runs with nothing uploaded at all, as a scripted walkthrough. But there is an upload bar, and this is the part people miss — give it a file and it stops being a cartoon.
Here is a customer churn file.
Two hundred and forty rows, nine features, and it has taken the last column, churned, as the label. Classification is already selected, because that column is a yes or no.

This is the screen. Four stages on a track — preprocess, feature engineering, feature selection, AutoML — and a data orb that travels to whichever one is running. Four, not the seven the Pipeline Builder lays out, because these are the four that visibly change the data itself.

Every scene calls the real backend on this file, and everything the narrator says is generated from what came back. The scenes are a fixed length whether a call takes half a second or twenty, so the animation is the loading state — there is no spinner anywhere in this tool.

You can pause it mid-scene, or stop it outright. And if a stage's call fails, that scene still plays with its scripted lines rather than the whole run dying at stage one — which matters on free hosting, where the first request has to wake a sleeping server.

And none of this is a stand-in. All four calls are the Pipeline Builder's own endpoints, on the same data, in the same order. The chapter before this one is the version you drive yourself — this is the version that explains itself while it runs.
Four scenes, four real calls, and the output of each one was the input to the next.
And the run is not thrown away when it ends. Click any stage and it opens again — here is AutoML, with the models it actually trained on this file, and the one that won.
